passage: Ira, you and Tara are shouting about the carrom rules again, so listen to your Nani. When I was ten, everyone called me Mahi, short for Mahima. My friend Shobha and I played hopscotch on the temple steps every evening. One day her stone landed on the line. "Out!" I said. "Line is in!" she said. We shouted until she kicked the stone away, and I nearly rubbed out her squares with my foot so I could win. Then old Bhola, the flower seller, called, "Each of you, say your rule once, and listen once." We did. In Shobha's village the line counted in; in mine it didn't. We chose her rule for that week and mine for the next, and Bhola kept score. We played that way for years.

qa.q: Where did Mahima and Shobha play hopscotch?
qa.a: They played hopscotch on the temple steps every evening.

qa.q: What was Mahima feeling when she nearly rubbed out Shobha's squares?
qa.a: Mahima felt angry and desperate to win, so frustrated that she almost cheated.

qa.q: Which choice in the story settled the argument, and why did it work?
qa.a: Each girl said her rule once and listened once, then they took turns with each rule; both felt heard, and Bhola kept it fair.

qa.q: How might Shobha have seen the moment her stone landed on the line?
qa.a: Shobha probably felt sure she was right, since in her village the line counted in, and felt cheated when Mahima called her out.

grounding: Shows two friends both claiming to be right in a game, then stating their views, listening and agreeing on a rule with a fair referee.

passage: Lunch break had four minutes left, and Afreen's team needed six runs off the last ball of the corridor cricket match. She swung hard; the tennis ball smacked the far wall. "Six!" she yelled. "Wall is four!" shouted Keerthana. "We said that yesterday!" Afreen's face went hot. She almost dropped the bat and walked off. Instead she took a breath. "I thought the wall was six because it's the boundary. Why four?" Keerthana explained that the wall was too close for a six. "Okay, I hear you. But we never agreed today." The bell was about to ring. They waved down Mr Pinto, the PE teacher, passing with his whistle. "New rule, both teams: wall is four, roof is six. Bowl the last ball again." Afreen groaned, then laughed and took guard.

qa.q: How many runs did Afreen's team need off the last ball?
qa.a: Afreen's team needed six runs.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling when her face went hot?
qa.a: Afreen felt angry and cheated, sure the shot was a six, and was tempted to quit.

qa.q: Which choice helped the friends settle the argument, and why?
qa.a: Afreen explained her view and asked for Keerthana's, then they asked Mr Pinto as a fair referee, so no one had to quit or cheat.

qa.q: How does Keerthana see Afreen asking "Why four?"
qa.a: Keerthana probably feels respected and calmer, since Afreen is listening instead of just shouting "Six!"

grounding: Illustrates friends arguing over a game rule under time pressure, hearing each other and asking a fair referee instead of quitting.

passage: In a Manchester park, Liam and Siddiq had jumpers for goalposts and a muddy football. Siddiq's shot flew over Liam's jumper. "Goal!" "That was over the post!" Liam said. "There's no post, so there's no height rule," Siddiq argued. It was 4–4, and the light was fading. Liam looked at his friend's grin, then at the sky. Winning a park match wasn't worth ten minutes of arguing, and Siddiq was moving to Leeds next month. "Fine, it counts," Liam said. "But after this, anything over the jumper is out." "Deal!" said Siddiq. They played until the streetlights came on, and by dinner Liam couldn't even remember the final score.

qa.q: What were Liam and Siddiq using for goalposts?
qa.a: They had jumpers for goalposts.

qa.q: Why did Liam let Siddiq's goal count?
qa.a: Liam cared more about the friendship than winning, especially with Siddiq moving to Leeds, and felt the argument wasn't worth it.

qa.q: What made Liam's compromise a smart one?
qa.a: He gave in on one small point but set a clear rule for the rest of the match, so the game stayed fair and fun.

qa.q: How might Siddiq see Liam saying "Fine, it counts"?
qa.a: Siddiq probably feels happy and grateful, and more willing to accept the new rule for the rest of the game.

grounding: Illustrates a child giving in on a small rule point to keep a game going, valuing the friendship over winning.

passage: In the girls' hostel common room, Hafsa and Harsha were halfway through a carrom game when Harsha pocketed the queen and then missed the cover. "Queen comes back," Hafsa said. "Not in my house rules. You keep it if you pot any piece after," said Harsha. The warden's lights-out bell was twenty minutes away. Hafsa thought of the night Harsha had sat up with her when she was homesick. It was only one queen. "Okay, your house rules tonight. Mine tomorrow?" Harsha laughed. "Deal." Hafsa lost by two points, but they were still giggling when the bell rang, and the next morning Harsha saved her a seat at breakfast.

qa.q: How long was it until the warden's lights-out bell?
qa.a: The bell was twenty minutes away.

qa.q: What was Hafsa thinking of when she decided to give in?
qa.a: Hafsa remembered Harsha sitting up with her when she was homesick and felt grateful, so one queen mattered less than the friendship.

qa.q: Why did "your house rules tonight, mine tomorrow" work well?
qa.a: It gave way on a small point while keeping things fair over time, so the game kept going and neither girl felt cheated.

qa.q: How does Harsha see Hafsa's offer?
qa.a: Harsha probably feels respected and warm toward Hafsa, which shows when she saves her a seat at breakfast.

grounding: Shows a child accepting a friend's rule on a small point so the game and the friendship stay warm.

passage:
Coach's note, junior chess club, Saturday (Coach Ramesh)
Yusuf lost to Ankita in round three. He swept his pieces off the board and said, "You only won because you got lucky, cheater." At lunch he told others not to sit with her. Ankita ate alone, eyes down.
I took Yusuf aside and asked what the game showed, not who she is. He admitted she spotted a fork he missed. I asked him to replay the game with her and find that move together. By the end they were arguing about openings, not about each other.
Plan: pair them for analysis again next week.

qa.q: In which round did Yusuf lose to Ankita?
qa.a: Yusuf lost to Ankita in round three.

qa.q: What was Yusuf feeling when he called Ankita a cheater?
qa.a: Yusuf felt angry and humiliated at losing, so he turned Ankita into an enemy instead of looking at the game.

qa.q: How did Coach Ramesh help Yusuf separate the game from the person?
qa.a: Coach Ramesh asked what the game showed rather than who Ankita was, then had them replay it together to find the fork.

qa.q: What was it like for Ankita when others were told not to sit with her?
qa.a: Ankita likely felt hurt and alone, eating with her eyes down, punished just for winning.

grounding: Illustrates a child treating the winner of a game as an enemy and taunting, and a coach helping separate the game from the person.

passage:
Thursday
Diary, I was horrible today. Nirmala beat me 21–18 in the badminton trials and got the last place in the school team. I told everyone her serve was illegal and did a silly copy of her celebration, and some kids laughed. She went red and left early. At home I couldn't eat. Papa asked what happened, and I said, "She's my enemy now." He said, "She beat your game, not you." That stuck. Her serve wasn't illegal; it was just better. Tomorrow I'll say sorry and ask how she does that flick. Maybe I'll make the team next term.
Francis

qa.q: What was the score when Nirmala beat Francis?
qa.a: Nirmala beat Francis 21–18 in the badminton trials.

qa.q: Why couldn't Francis eat at home that evening?
qa.a: Francis felt guilty and ashamed about taunting Nirmala, and was still stung by losing the team place.

qa.q: What small step is Francis planning, and why is it wise?
qa.a: Francis plans to say sorry and ask Nirmala about her flick, turning a rival into someone to learn from instead of an enemy.

qa.q: How might Nirmala have felt when people laughed at the copied celebration?
qa.a: Nirmala probably felt humiliated and hurt, which is why she went red and left early.

grounding: Shows a child taunting a rival who won, then learning to separate the game from the person before a grudge sets in.

passage: At the school science fair prize-giving, Ujjwal clapped as his best friend Anjali walked up for first prize with her water-filter model. His own solar oven had come fourth. His chest felt tight and proud at the same time: he had helped her sand the charcoal box, and she had practised her talk on him all week. When she came back, eyes shining, he made himself stand up. "You were brilliant. Congratulations." Then, quieter: "Can you show me how you practised your talk? Mine was all mumbles." Anjali grinned. "Saturday, your house?" On the bus home, Ujjwal made a list: practise aloud, time it, ask two questions.

qa.q: What place did Ujjwal's solar oven get?
qa.a: Ujjwal's solar oven came fourth.

qa.q: What was Ujjwal feeling as Anjali walked up for first prize?
qa.a: Ujjwal felt a sting of jealousy and real pride at once, since he had helped her with the charcoal box.

qa.q: How did Ujjwal turn his envy into something useful?
qa.a: He congratulated Anjali sincerely, asked how she practised her talk and made a plan to practise aloud and time himself.

qa.q: How does Anjali see Ujjwal's congratulations?
qa.a: Anjali likely feels happy and supported by her best friend, which is why she offers to help on Saturday 😊

grounding: Illustrates a child feeling jealousy and pride when a best friend wins, congratulating her and using it as a push to practise.

passage: I'm Tenzin, and I sit behind Irfan in 6B. When the headmistress announced that Eshaan had won the inter-school drawing prize, Irfan's jaw went tight, and he pressed his pencil so hard the tip snapped. For a second I thought he might walk out. Eshaan is his best friend; they draw comics together at every break. Then Irfan stood up, hugged Eshaan and shouted, "Told you your dragon was the best!" He sounded happy. He also didn't talk much at lunch. That week I saw him in the art room every break, redrawing the same hand again and again. I don't know exactly what he felt, but he kept going.

qa.q: What happened when Irfan pressed his pencil hard?
qa.a: Irfan pressed his pencil so hard the tip snapped.

qa.q: What might Irfan have been feeling when his jaw went tight?
qa.a: Irfan probably felt a sting of envy mixed with pride for his best friend, though Tenzin can't be sure.

qa.q: What did Irfan do that turned the moment into progress?
qa.a: He congratulated Eshaan openly and then practised in the art room every break, using the sting as a push to improve.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see Irfan's hug and shout?
qa.a: Eshaan likely feels proud and glad that his best friend cheered for him, and may not notice the quieter lunch.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's eyes, a child's mixed envy and pride at a best friend's win, followed by congratulations and practice.

passage: When Salma won the inter-school essay prize, Joseph was sure it was unfair. "Her tuition sir wrote it," he whispered to three classmates by the water cooler of their Pune school. By Friday the rumour had spread through Class 7. Salma stopped answering in class. But Joseph felt worse, not better. He kept checking who was talking about it, couldn't enjoy the cricket match on Saturday, and lay awake replaying her name being called. On Monday Salma read her essay aloud in assembly, stumbling over a line she had clearly written herself, about her Ammi's sewing machine. Joseph's ears burned. The grudge had eaten his whole weekend and hadn't changed the prize at all.

qa.q: What did Joseph whisper to three classmates?
qa.a: Joseph whispered, "Her tuition sir wrote it."

qa.q: Why did Joseph's ears burn when Salma read her essay?
qa.a: Joseph felt ashamed, realising the essay was clearly her own and his rumour was unfair.

qa.q: What could Joseph do now to repair things?
qa.a: Joseph could tell the three classmates the rumour was wrong and apologise to Salma, rather than keep carrying the grudge.

qa.q: How might Salma have felt during the week of the rumour?
qa.a: Salma probably felt hurt and embarrassed, which is why she stopped answering in class.

grounding: Illustrates a child who believes a rival's win was unfair, spreads gossip, and finds the resentment hurts him more than her.

passage:
"Swati only won the singing prize because the judge is her mother's friend."
"Who told you that?"
"Everyone knows."
"Sabina, I asked around. Nobody knows. You started it on Monday."
"Well, she can't even hold the high note properly."
"She held it for ages. We all heard."
"..."
"You've talked about Swati every break this week. You didn't even eat your paratha today."
"Because it's not fair!"
"Or because you wanted it really badly?"
"...I practised every day, Ruth."
"I know. So did she. Being angry at her isn't making you sing better. It's making you miserable."
"Maybe I should stop saying the judge thing."
"Maybe you should tell people it wasn't true."

qa.q: What did Sabina claim about the judge?
qa.a: Sabina said the judge is Swati's mother's friend.

qa.q: What does Sabina's "...I practised every day" reveal about how she feels?
qa.a: It reveals Sabina feels hurt and disappointed at losing after so much practice, and that envy lies under her anger at Swati.

qa.q: What small step would help Sabina now?
qa.a: Telling people the judge story wasn't true, as Ruth suggests, would stop the harm and free Sabina from the grudge.

qa.q: How might Swati experience the rumour if she hears it?
qa.a: Swati would likely feel hurt and insulted that her hard-won prize was called unfair.

grounding: Shows a child spreading gossip that a rival's win was unfair, and a friend helping her see the resentment hurts her most.

passage: At their primary school in Lisbon, Beatriz won the class maths puzzle race for the third time. Chen, who always finished fifth or sixth, didn't feel angry. He felt curious. How did she do it so fast? At break he watched her doodle quick little tables in the margin before each puzzle. "Can I ask how you practise?" he said, pulling up a stool. Beatriz looked surprised, then pleased. "Ten puzzles every night, and I always check the easy ones first." Chen wrote it on his hand. That evening he did ten puzzles at the kitchen table, drawing little tables just like hers.

qa.q: How many puzzles does Beatriz practise every night?
qa.a: Beatriz does ten puzzles every night.

qa.q: What was Chen feeling when Beatriz won again?
qa.a: Chen felt curious and admiring rather than angry, wanting to learn how she solved puzzles so fast.

qa.q: Which choice by Chen worked, and why?
qa.a: Watching her method and then asking politely for tips gave Chen a real practice plan to copy.

qa.q: How does Beatriz see Chen asking about her practice?
qa.a: Beatriz is surprised and pleased, probably proud that someone values her effort.

grounding: Illustrates a child admiring a classmate's win, studying how she practised and asking for tips.

passage: At the Saturday music school in Mysuru, Eshaan's name was read out as winner of the junior tabla contest. Rukmini clapped the loudest. She had heard him from the practice room for months, playing the same eight beats slowly, then faster, then slowly again. After the certificates, she found him packing his drums. "How did you get your tirakita so clean? Mine sounds like rain on a tin roof." Eshaan laughed. "Guruji made me use a metronome at half speed for a month. So boring." "Can you show me?" He set it ticking. Rukmini copied him, beat by slow beat, until the caretaker came to lock up.

qa.q: What contest did Eshaan win?
qa.a: Eshaan won the junior tabla contest.

qa.q: Why did Rukmini clap the loudest?
qa.a: Rukmini admired Eshaan, having heard him practise the same eight beats for months, and felt happy for him.

qa.q: What small step helped Rukmini learn from Eshaan?
qa.a: She asked him a specific question about his tirakita and then copied his half-speed metronome practice right away.

qa.q: How might Eshaan see Rukmini's question?
qa.a: Eshaan probably feels flattered and friendly, glad to share the boring trick that worked for him.

grounding: Shows a child turning admiration for a winner into a role model by asking how he practised and copying it.

passage: In the library period, Kiran Ma'am handed back Sudha's story with red notes: "Strong ending. Opening is slow; start with action. Cut the poem at the start." Sudha read it twice. She admired Kiran Ma'am, who wrote stories for a children's magazine. She raised her hand. "Ma'am, what counts as action? Can it be someone speaking?" "Yes, a line of dialogue works well." Sudha hesitated. "I'd like to keep the poem, though. It's my Nani's, and the ending comes back to it." Kiran Ma'am tapped her pen. "Fair point. Keep it, but move it after the first scene." That evening Sudha rewrote the opening, starting with Nani's voice calling from the well.

qa.q: What did Kiran Ma'am say about Sudha's opening?
qa.a: Kiran Ma'am wrote that the opening is slow; start with action.

qa.q: Why did Sudha hesitate before asking to keep the poem?
qa.a: Sudha admired Kiran Ma'am and felt nervous about disagreeing, but the poem mattered because it was her Nani's.

qa.q: What made Sudha's response to the feedback wise?
qa.a: She asked a follow-up question, used the advice that evening, and disagreed on one point politely, with a reason.

qa.q: How does Kiran Ma'am see Sudha's disagreement?
qa.a: Kiran Ma'am sees it as a fair, thoughtful point and adjusts the advice, respecting Sudha's reason.

grounding: Illustrates a child treating a teacher's feedback as guidance, asking a follow-up, applying it and disagreeing honestly on one point.

passage: I'm Sachin, Vaibhav's bench partner in 5C. When Mrs Kulkarni returned our maths tests, she had written on Vaibhav's: "Right answers, but show your working." He frowned, and I thought he'd sulk like I did. Instead he went to her desk. "Ma'am, if I can do it in my head, why write it?" She said working shows where mistakes hide. He nodded slowly, then said, "But for easy sums, can I skip it?" She smiled. "For one-step sums, yes." In the next test, Vaibhav filled every margin with neat steps, and he caught his own mistake in question six before handing it in. I still don't know if he agreed with all of it.

qa.q: What had Mrs Kulkarni written on Vaibhav's test?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni wrote, "Right answers, but show your working."

qa.q: What might Vaibhav have been feeling when he frowned at the note?
qa.a: Vaibhav probably felt puzzled and a little annoyed, but curious enough to ask why rather than sulk.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav's questions help him?
qa.a: Asking why and gently pushing back on easy sums got him a clear reason and a fair rule, which helped him catch his own mistake in question six.

qa.q: How might Mrs Kulkarni see Vaibhav's "why"?
qa.a: Mrs Kulkarni likely sees it as respectful curiosity, since she answers kindly and even agrees about one-step sums.

grounding: Shows, through a classmate's account, a child asking why about a teacher's feedback, disagreeing politely on one point and applying it.

passage:
Tuesday night
Vaibhav Sir gave my Hindi composition a C again and wrote "careless matras" all over it. He never smiles at me. I think he just doesn't like me, so this week I didn't even do the practice sheet. What's the point?
But today Ammi read the comments with me. She pointed out he'd also written "good ideas, lively story" in small letters at the bottom. I hadn't even seen that. Ammi said, "He's marking your matras, not you." Maybe she's right. The matras really are messy.
Plan: redo the practice sheet tomorrow and check every matra before I hand in.
Zainab

qa.q: What grade did Vaibhav Sir give Zainab's Hindi composition?
qa.a: Vaibhav Sir gave it a C again.

qa.q: Why did Zainab stop doing the practice sheet?
qa.a: Zainab felt resentful and hurt, believing Vaibhav Sir disliked Zainab, so trying seemed pointless.

qa.q: What helped Zainab separate the feedback from the person?
qa.a: Reading the comments with Ammi showed the praise for Zainab's ideas and that the criticism was only about matras.

qa.q: How might Vaibhav Sir see Zainab's missing practice sheet?
qa.a: Vaibhav Sir might think Zainab has stopped caring, not knowing the C made Zainab feel disliked.

grounding: Illustrates a child who thinks the teacher dislikes them and stops trying, then learns to separate the feedback from the person.

passage: In the one-room school at the edge of the village, Manjula Teacher stopped Afreen halfway through her reading. "Too fast. Again, slowly." Some boys at the back sniggered. Afreen decided Manjula Teacher hated her. For two weeks she kept her head down and never offered to read. Then one afternoon she heard the teacher stop Gopal, the best reader in class, with the same words: "Too fast. Again." Gopal just read it again, slower, and got a nod. After school, Afreen lingered by the door. "Teacher, do you think I read badly?" "You read well, Afreen. Just too fast for others to follow." The next morning, Afreen's hand went up first.

qa.q: What did Manjula Teacher tell Afreen halfway through her reading?
qa.a: Manjula Teacher said, "Too fast. Again, slowly."

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling during the two weeks she kept her head down?
qa.a: Afreen felt resentful and embarrassed, believing Manjula Teacher hated her after the sniggering.

qa.q: What helped Afreen separate the feedback from the person?
qa.a: Hearing the same words given to Gopal, then asking Manjula Teacher directly, showed the comment was about speed, not about Afreen.

qa.q: How might Manjula Teacher see Afreen's question at the door?
qa.a: Manjula Teacher probably feels glad Afreen asked, and may realise the correction stung more than intended.

grounding: Shows a child who believes the teacher dislikes her and stops trying, until she sees the feedback is about the reading, not her.

passage:
Sunday
Dadi taught me to plant methi on the balcony today. Before I could pour the seeds in, she said, "Soak them overnight first, and sow them thin, not in a heap." I wanted to say my science teacher never mentioned soaking, but I let her finish. She has grown vegetables since she was my age, in her village near Nashik.
Then I asked, "Dadi, why soak them?" She laughed. "Hard seeds wake up faster in water. Try both and see." So we set up an experiment: one pot soaked, one pot dry. I'm writing it in my science notebook too.
Ishita

qa.q: Where did Dadi grow vegetables when she was young?
qa.a: Dadi grew vegetables in her village near Nashik.

qa.q: Why did Ishita let Dadi finish before asking?
qa.a: Ishita respected Dadi's years of growing vegetables, yet felt curious about the soaking, so Ishita waited and then asked politely.

qa.q: What is clever about the two-pot plan?
qa.a: Soaking one pot and not the other lets Ishita test Dadi's advice respectfully while learning from it.

qa.q: How might Dadi see Ishita's "why"?
qa.a: Dadi seems pleased and amused, happy to explain and even suggesting the test herself.

grounding: Illustrates a child listening to a grandparent without interrupting, valuing her experience and still asking why politely.

passage: On the farm near Hoshiarpur, Preeti and her cousin Kiran were about to climb the old mango tree when Nana called from his charpai. "Not today, puttar. Wait till the sun dries the bark." Kiran groaned, but Preeti walked over and sat on the edge of the charpai until Nana had finished. Then she asked, "Nana, why the sun? The branches look strong." Nana pointed with his stick. "Wet bark is slippery as soap, and red ants climb up after rain. I fell from that very tree when I was your age." Preeti looked at the shiny trunk. "Can we climb tomorrow afternoon, then?" "Tomorrow afternoon," Nana agreed.

qa.q: What did Nana say climbs up after rain?
qa.a: Nana said red ants climb up after rain.

qa.q: What was Preeti feeling when she asked "why the sun?"
qa.a: Preeti felt curious and a little doubtful, since the branches looked strong, but asked politely out of respect for Nana.

qa.q: Which choice by Preeti worked better than Kiran's groan?
qa.a: Preeti listened to the end and then asked why, so she got a real reason and a plan to climb tomorrow.

qa.q: How might Nana see Preeti sitting and waiting until he finished?
qa.a: Nana likely feels respected and glad to share his own story of falling from the tree.

grounding: Shows a child listening fully to a grandfather's advice and then asking why, so respect and curiosity sit together.

passage:
Wednesday
Ammi gave me the school bag speech AGAIN tonight: pack at night, check the timetable, blah blah. I rolled my eyes so hard Neelam Apa laughed. Ammi's face went tight, and I knew a longer speech was coming.
Before it did, I remembered what Apa told me last week: "Say you heard her, then ask to try your way." So I said, "Ammi, I heard you. Can I try packing in the morning for one week? If I forget something, I'll do it your way." Ammi blinked. Then she said, "One week. Deal."
No shouting, no sulking. Weirdly, I felt taller.
Irfan

qa.q: What did Irfan ask to try for one week?
qa.a: Irfan asked to try packing in the morning for one week.

qa.q: What was Irfan feeling when Ammi gave the school bag speech again?
qa.a: Irfan felt irritated and lectured, which showed in the big eye-roll.

qa.q: Why did "I heard you" plus a one-week test work?
qa.a: It showed Ammi she was heard and offered a fair test with a backup plan, so she could agree instead of lecturing more.

qa.q: How might Ammi feel when Irfan offers the one-week deal?
qa.a: Ammi is probably surprised and relieved, and respects Irfan for answering calmly instead of sulking.

grounding: Illustrates a child who feels lectured and rolls their eyes, then says "I heard you, let me try my way" instead of sulking.

passage: At the family fruit stall in Malegaon, Abbu was explaining for the third time how to stack the bananas. "Big ones at the back, small in front, never bruise them, customers see everything." Rafiq rolled his eyes and muttered, "I know, Abbu." His friend Tarun, waiting with his cycle, grinned. Abbu's voice rose. "You know? Then why were yesterday's all bruised?" Rafiq felt his face go hot. He wanted to storm off to Tarun's cycle. Instead he took a breath. "Abbu, I heard you. Let me stack them my way today, in basket rows, and you check at noon." Abbu paused, then waved a hand. "Noon." At noon, he nodded at the neat rows.

qa.q: When did Rafiq ask Abbu to check the bananas?
qa.a: Rafiq asked Abbu to check at noon.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when he rolled his eyes and muttered?
qa.a: Rafiq felt irritated and lectured after hearing the stacking rules for the third time.

qa.q: What small step helped Rafiq avoid a fight?
qa.a: He took a breath, said he heard Abbu, and asked to try his own way with a check at noon, instead of storming off.

qa.q: How might Abbu see Rafiq's offer?
qa.a: Abbu may feel his advice was heard at last and is willing to trust Rafiq, especially after seeing the neat rows.

grounding: Shows a child irritated by a parent's repeated advice who says he heard it and asks to try his own way instead of storming off.
